title: Report Writing and Summarisation — news & event report format
notes: **What it is:** factual, third-person, past-tense reporting of an event (sports day, blood donation camp) — not a story, not an opinion.

**Structure:** Headline (short, factual) → Byline ('By a Staff Reporter') + dateline ('Kathmandu, 12 May:') → Lead paragraph answering WHO did WHAT, WHERE, WHEN, WHY in 2–3 sentences → Body in chronological order → a short quotation from the chief guest → closing outcome.
**Tense/voice grammar:** past simple for every event; passive voice is standard for ceremony facts ('trophies were distributed'); reported speech for quotes; third person only — never 'I'.
**Summarisation partner skill:** compress any passage into its core idea in your own words within the word limit — keep the author's viewpoint, drop examples and repetition.
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

**Complete event report template:**
[HEADLINE: Short, factual — 5-8 words, present simple]
By [a Staff Reporter / The Correspondent]
[City], [Date]:

[Lead paragraph: WHO attended, WHAT happened, WHERE, WHEN, WHY — 3-4 sentences max. This is the most important paragraph — write it first.]

[Body paragraph 1: Chronological sequence of events — opening ceremony, key activities, guest interactions]

[Body paragraph 2: More details — speeches given, performances, participant numbers, highlights]

[Optional: Quotation from chief guest or dignitary in reported speech]

[Closing paragraph: Outcome — results, conclusion, future plans, or next event.]

**No personal opinion. No 'I'. Past tense throughout.**

**Headline writing — the newswriter's craft:** A good headline: (1) Captures the main event in 5-8 words; (2) Uses present simple tense ('School Holds Annual Sports Day'); (3) Avoids full stops and unnecessary words; (4) Contains the who/what of the event; (5) Is factual, not sensational ('Explosion Rocks City' is tabloid; 'Annual Science Exhibition Held' is factual report). Bad: 'Incredible Day at School!' Good: 'Annual Sports Day Celebrated at St. Xavier School.'

**Dateline — the anchor of location and time:** Always format as: [City], [Day] [Month] [Date]:. Example: 'Kathmandu, 15 March:' or 'Pokhara, 2 January:'. The dateline appears immediately after the byline and before the lead paragraph. It tells the reader exactly WHERE and WHEN the event took place — essential for a news report.

**Lead paragraph — the inverted pyramid apex:** Journalists use the 'inverted pyramid' structure: most important info first, least important last. The lead (first paragraph) MUST answer: WHO (who was there/organised), WHAT (what happened), WHERE (location), WHEN (date/time), and WHY (purpose). Combine all five in 2-3 sentences. Everything that follows adds detail. If the report is cut short from the bottom, the lead still makes sense.

**Body paragraphs — chronological reporting:** Report bodies follow time order: 'The event commenced at…', 'Following the inaugural address, the chief guest…', 'After the prize distribution, the guests…', 'The programme concluded with…' Use time markers: 'first', 'then', 'afterwards', 'meanwhile', 'later', 'finally'. Each body paragraph covers one phase of the event. Be specific: '200 students from 12 schools' is better than 'many students'.

**Quotations — using reported speech in reports:** Reports use reported (indirect) speech for quotes, not direct speech with quotation marks. 'The chief guest, in his address, said that education was the key to national development. He added that students should read beyond the textbook.' Never: 'The chief guest said,
' In exams, this distinction is often tested. Keep the verb tense consistent: past tense ('said that… was…') in reports.

**Passive voice — the report's natural voice:** Reports prefer passive voice for actions performed on objects: 'The prize money was distributed among the winners', 'Certificates were handed over by the chief guest', 'The flag was hoisted by the principal'. Use active voice when the person matters: 'The principal delivered the welcome address' (person is important). The rule of thumb: passive for ceremony/objective facts, active for people/speakers.

**Summarisation — the partner skill:** A summary condenses a passage into its essential meaning in your own words. Method: (1) Read the passage fully once; (2) Identify the main idea (usually in the first or last sentence of each paragraph); (3) Note key supporting points; (4) Draft by combining main ideas + key supports in your own words; (5) Cut to fit word limit (usually 80-100 words for a 300-word passage); (6) Check: is every word essential? Could it be shortened? NEVER copy whole sentences. NEVER add opinion. NEVER include examples or anecdotes.

**Summary word-count discipline:** If asked to summarise in 'about 80 words', 70-90 is acceptable. 60 is too short (you've omitted key ideas); 100 is too long (you've included non-essentials). Count your words. Practice counting accurately — it's a skill tested in NEB exams. A summary should be approximately 1/4 to 1/3 the length of the original passage.

**Summarisation techniques for exam mastery:** (1) *Generalisation*: 'The boy ate apples, oranges, and bananas' → 'The boy ate various fruits.' (2) *Nominalisation*: 'The government decided to reduce taxes' → 'The government's tax reduction decision.' (3) *Merging*: Combine two related sentences into one. (4) *Omission*: Delete examples, repetitions, anecdotes. (5) *Simplification*: Replace complex descriptions with single words. (6) *Abstraction*: Replace specific lists with categories.

**Note-making — the structured summary:** Notes are a visual summary of a passage. Format: TITLE (in caps) → numbered sub-headings (1, 2, 3) for each paragraph/section → lettered points (a, b, c) under each sub-heading → abbreviations list at bottom. Keep each point to under 7 words. Use arrows (→), ampersands (&), etc. Notes are tested for: accuracy of sub-headings, completeness of key ideas, conciseness of points, correct abbreviation usage.

**Note-making rules and conventions:** (1) Title: UPPERCASE, capture the main theme. (2) Sub-headings: Numbered (1, 2, 3), in NOUN PHRASE form (not sentences). (3) Points: Lettered (a, b, c), in KEY PHRASES (not full sentences). (4) No full stops in sub-headings or points. (5) Abbreviations defined at bottom (govt., approx., vs., etc.). (6) Each point under 7 words. (7) Maintain the original order of ideas. (8) Do not add your own interpretation.

**Common report writing errors:** (1) First-person narration ('I attended the function') — never 'I' in a report. (2) Past tense used inconsistently — switch between past and present. (3) Opinion or commentary ('It was the best event ever') — reports are objective. (4) Direct speech quotes instead of reported speech. (5) Missing headline or dateline. (6) Chronological confusion — jumping between time periods. (7) Too much detail / missing key facts. (8) Emotional language ('Heartbreaking tragedy', 'Amazing success').

**Report vs. Story — the key difference:** A report tells WHAT happened; a story tells HOW it felt. A report is objective and external; a story is subjective and internal. A report uses past tense, third person, and passive voice; a story uses past tense, first/third person, and active voice. A report includes facts, numbers, and quotes; a story includes emotions, dialogue, and sensory detail. In exams, confusing these loses the 'form' marks immediately.

**Note-taking with abbreviations — speed writing:** In exams, abbreviations earn marks when defined. Standard abbreviations: acc. (according), approx. (approximately),Assoc. (Association), b/c (because), Dept. (Department), e.g. (for example), Govt. (Government), in (in), i.e. (that is), incl. (including), opp. (opposite), org. (organisation), ppl (people), resp. (responsible), sq. km (square kilometre), vs. (versus), wrt (with regard to). Never use abbreviations in the TITLE or SUB-HEADING — only in the bullet points.

**Event report practice checklist:** Before submitting your report, verify: [ ] Headline present and factual [ ] Byline + dateline present [ ] Lead answers WHO, WHAT, WHERE, WHEN, WHY [ ] Body is chronological [ ] Quotation in reported speech [ ] No first person, no opinion [ ] Past tense throughout [ ] Closing paragraph with outcome [ ] Within word limit [ ] Spelling checked.
confusion: Report vs. Summary: A report writes about an EVENT that happened (news report). A summary condenses a GIVEN PASSAGE into fewer words. Both use third person and past tense, but they have different purposes and structures. Reports create new content from observed facts; summaries repackage existing text.
Reported speech vs. Direct speech in reports: Reports use reported speech ('The guest said that…') for quotes. Direct speech ('The guest said,
') is for feature articles and stories, not formal event reports. This distinction is frequently tested in NEB exams.

Note-making vs. Summary: Notes are a VISUAL, STRUCTURED format with numbered sub-headings and lettered points. A summary is a PARAGRAPH of continuous prose. Notes use abbreviations and fragments; summaries use full sentences. Both condense the same passage, but the output format differs.

Lead paragraph vs. Introduction: In a report, the lead paragraph is the FIRST paragraph — it must answer all five Ws (who, what, where, when, why). In an essay, the introduction sets up the topic and thesis. The report lead is factual and dense; the essay introduction is engaging and argumentative.

Dateline vs. Date in letter format: In a report, the dateline is part of the header format: 'Kathmandu, 15 March:' — it runs inline with the byline. In a formal letter, the date is on its own line below the sender's address. Never format a report date like a letter date.
practice: Write a news report (200-250 words) about a national blood donation camp held at your school. Include: headline, byline, dateline, lead paragraph with all 5 Ws, chronological body, reported speech quotation from the chief guest, and outcome. Use passive voice for ceremony facts.

Summarise the following passage (150 words) into 60 words: 'Climate change refers to significant changes in global temperature, precipitation, and wind patterns over several decades. While some climate change is natural, scientific evidence shows that human activities — burning fossil fuels, deforestation, and industrial processes — have accelerated warming since the Industrial Revolution. The consequences include rising sea levels, more frequent extreme weather events, and disruptions to ecosystems.'

Make notes from the following passage (180 words) on 'The Importance of Rivers for Human Civilisation': Identify the title, numbered sub-headings, lettered points, and write an abbreviations list. Keep each point under 7 words.

Read the given passage about 'Urban Air Pollution' and write a summary (80 words) in your own words. Then identify three summarisation techniques you used (generalisation, nominalisation, omission, etc.).

Write a note-making exercise on 'The Advantages and Disadvantages of Social Media'. Divide into 3 numbered sections: (1) Social benefits, (2) Psychological effects, (3) Societal concerns. List 3 lettered points under each with abbreviations. Define your abbreviations.
universalFacts: The inverted pyramid structure — most important information first, details after — originated with Civil War-era journalists who had to cut stories from the bottom when telegraph lines failed. It remains the standard structure for news reports worldwide.

In the NEB English exam, report writing typically carries 8-10 marks, while summarisation carries 5-8 marks. Together they test the student's ability to process and reorganise information — a core academic skill.

The term 'dateline' originally referred to the line in a newspaper article that stated both the location and date of the report: 'Kathmandu, May 15 —'. Modern news media sometimes include just the location, but exams expect both.

Note-making as a skill was formalised in the early 20th century as a study technique. Modern shorthand systems (like Pitman's) influenced the style: abbreviations, symbols, and fragmented phrases that capture the maximum meaning in minimum space.

Summarisation is one of the most commonly tested skills across all English exams worldwide (CBSE, ICSE, Cambridge, NEB, IELTS, TOEFL). The 1/4 to 1/3 length rule and the 'own words' requirement are universal standards — mastering this one skill benefits every English assessment.
